glossary.extended_explanation: Memex is useful as a reference point when discussing systems that preserve not just documents, but the relationships between documents. The important idea is that knowledge becomes more valuable when it can be connected, revisited, and navigated through links rather than stored as isolated files. In modern AI workflows, the Memex analogy helps frame retrieval, linking, and synthesis as parts of a persistent knowledge environment rather than one-off question answering.
glossary.proposed_definition: A hypothetical personal knowledge machine proposed by Vannevar Bush in 1945 for storing information and linking related ideas through associative trails. It is often used as an early conceptual ancestor of hypertext and personal knowledge systems.
glossary.relevance_note: Useful for understanding the historical lineage of linked knowledge systems and why persistent cross-referenced context is valuable in AI-assisted documentation and support tooling.
glossary.supporting_snippet: Karpathy mentions in his original document that this idea is related to Vannevar Bush’s Memex from 1945 — a vision of a personal knowledge store with “associative trails” between documents.

glossary.extended_explanation: A personal knowledge base is more than a folder of notes. Its job is to preserve useful context, make related information easy to find, and accumulate understanding across projects or time. In AI workflows, it becomes especially useful when an assistant can ingest sources, maintain structure, and update pages automatically so the knowledge store stays coherent.
glossary.proposed_definition: A system for collecting, organizing, linking, and retrieving information for an individual or small team over time. It typically combines source capture, structured notes, cross-references, and search.
glossary.relevance_note: This is a durable concept for AI-assisted documentation, research, onboarding, and support operations, where information must accumulate instead of getting lost in chat history.
glossary.supporting_snippet: It was just an idea — written in plain markdown describing a pattern for how to use AI agents to build and maintain personal knowledge bases.

how_to.answer_summary: Keep the original documents in a read-only raw source folder, let the AI generate and own the wiki folder, and define the workflow in a schema file that tells the agent what page types exist and how to update them. Ingest each new source into the wiki, then have the agent update existing pages, create new ones only when needed, add glossary terms, and log the changes. Add a lint pass so the system can detect contradictions, stale claims, orphan pages, and missing links. The key practice is to treat the wiki as the persistent artifact and the raw documents as immutable inputs.
how_to.caveats: The article’s evidence is a small personal build, so scaling, permissions, and reliability across many authors or many thousands of documents remain open questions.

source_summary.summary: The article describes a personal knowledge-base workflow inspired by Andrej Karpathy’s llm-wiki.md idea: store raw sources separately, have an AI read them once, and maintain a structured wiki that grows over time. The core claim is that knowledge work fails less because of missing information than because of maintenance overhead: cross-references, summaries, glossary updates, contradiction checks, and page linking become too expensive for humans to sustain. The author reports building a working repo in Cursor plus Obsidian in about 30 minutes, using a schema file (CLAUDE.md) that defines page types and workflows. The resulting system supports ingest, query, and lint operations, and the wiki becomes the persistent artifact rather than chat history or raw documents. The article frames this as a practical answer to the problem of stale wikis and scattered project knowledge.
source_summary.why_it_matters: As of 2026-04-07, this is a concrete pattern for turning scattered project documents into a living knowledge system that can be maintained by AI with less manual bookkeeping. That matters for AI engineering and service organizations because most internal knowledge bases fail on upkeep, not on initial creation. The article’s durable lesson is that the workflow and schema matter as much as the model: if the AI can reliably ingest, link, summarize, and lint, the knowledge base can stay usable longer. This is especially relevant for teams managing product documentation, support playbooks, onboarding material, and cross-functional research.

llm_item.knowledge_summary: AI-maintained knowledge bases are systems where an AI ingests source material, synthesizes structured pages, and updates links and summaries as new information arrives. The durable value comes from maintenance: the AI is used not only for extraction, but also for keeping the knowledge base coherent, current, and interconnected. These systems work best when raw inputs are preserved separately from generated knowledge and when page types and update rules are explicitly defined. A lightweight but disciplined structure can reduce the manual burden that normally causes wikis to stagnate.
llm_item.operational_insight: Use AI to automate the bookkeeping layer of knowledge work, but keep the schema and ownership boundaries explicit so updates remain trustworthy.
llm_item.relevance_note: This captures the core reusable pattern behind AI-assisted documentation systems, support knowledge bases, and internal research repositories.
llm_item.supporting_snippet: LLM Wiki flips this around. Instead of searching your raw documents every time, the AI reads your documents once and builds a structured wiki from them... When you add a new document, the AI doesn’t start over. It reads the new source and updates the existing wiki, adding to pages that already exist, creating new ones where needed, flagging contradictions, and keeping everything consistent.

llm_item.knowledge_summary: A schema-driven agent workflow uses a machine-readable or instruction-file schema to constrain what an AI agent can create, update, or check. The schema acts as the operational contract: it defines entity types, page formats, step order, and validation behavior. This reduces prompt drift and makes the agent more predictable across repeated runs. In practice, schema-driven workflows are especially valuable when the agent must maintain state across many files or many sessions.
llm_item.operational_insight: If an AI is responsible for maintaining a knowledge system, define the workflow in a schema file before asking it to generate content.
llm_item.relevance_note: This is broadly useful for AI engineering teams that want repeatable agent behavior rather than one-off chat outputs.
llm_item.supporting_snippet: Think of it as the rulebook that turns a general-purpose AI into a disciplined wiki maintainer.
